The United States Navy wants to fill the vacant places in the ranks and wants it does quickly. The recruiting campaign now being carried on by Uncels Sam's naval officers is on with a rush and is sweeping the country from coast to coast.

The aeroplan is the latest means adopted by the officers to aid them in their reciprocity work.

THE NEWEST ADDITION TO UCLE SAM'S NAVY--AIRPLANE CARRIER.

378,415. Photographed on the eve of her christening by the wife of the Secretary of the Navy, Mrs. Curtis D. Wilbur, photo shows the S.S. Saratoga, and airplane carrier which is the newest addition to the Navy. She was built by the New York Shipbuilding Company and is shown on the ways at Camden, N.Y., with the New Jersey Shore in the background.
PROPOSED AIRPLANE CARRIER.

One of the two airplane carriers which are now building, which were originally intended to be the Saratoga, and Lexington, until the Arms Parley forced them to be turned into plane carriers. They will be literally floating airplane fields. They will also be floating electric generating plants. As naval vessels they will be the longest in the world. With a power of four times the Maryland they will make a speed of over thirty three knots. They will be 850 feet long. They are both electrically equipped and drive. The vessels will exemplify the last word in radio equipment. The decks will be as immense and max unobstructed that they will resemble a small-sized drill ground. 11/28/22
UNITED STATES STARTS TRAINING AVILATORS AT SIGNAL CORPS SCHOOL AT MINBOLA, L.I.

The United States has begun training reserve millimilitary aviators subject to call in time of war. The first quota were distributed among the three aviation schools on the Atlantic seabard. They will undergo six months training at their stations. Nine men have started at the Signal Corps school at Mineola, IL. They are being carefully instructed in all branches of flying and in the details and mechanism of the machines.

Actual flying of course forms a great part of the instructive program but they spend many hours in the shops learning how to repair, take apart, and put together their motors, and other working machinery. The students are also taught how to construct minor parts of the machines.

The photograph shows men of the school examining instruments on deck and in cockpit just before making a flight. This inspection is made to insure safety and is repeated every time an ascension is made.

Fully loaded it weighs 15 inches. Over five inches of 1, which is useful load the wing span 1.26 feet the width of the span is 12 feet and the length of the fuselage is 65 feet.

One of these machines flew from Ipswich, England to India a distance of 5800 miles last winter and covered 700 miles of the trip over the Mediterranean which was a record flight for a land machine flying over water.

This type of machine will be used to a very large extent in Commercial aviation bring able to carry a five ton load up of people, mail or merchandise in a non-stop flight between Boston and St.Louis within twelve hours.

UNITED STATES WORLD FLYERS ARRIVE.

The American world-flyers arrived at Waddington Aerodrome, Crzydon, from Paris, this afternoon (July 16th), and were given a tremendous reception by hundreds of American and British people. One of the most interested spectators on the aerodrome was Mrs. Maclaren, wife of SQuadron-Leader MacLaren, leader of the Britishworld-flight attempt.

AMERICAN WORLD FLYERS PHOTOGRAPHERD ON RETURN TO BOSTON! O.R.S., The U.S. Army planes "Chicago" and "New Orleans" lighting on the 5 months and 14 days after departing from the United States at Santa Monica, on a world tour, which they successfully completed!

Lieut. John A. Macready and Oakley G.Kelly, U.S.A., holders of many aerial records hopped off from Curtiss Filed, Long Island, at 1:37 o'clock this afternoon in an attempt to cross the continent to San Diego, Cal., in a non-stop flight. After taking aborad their fuel, food etc they hopped off at exactly 1:37, expecting to reach their destination shortly after noon tomorrow. Their machine is a monoplane of the Fokker type, loaded with 737 gallons of gasoline, cooked rations for two days, two gallons of coffee in thermos bottles the entire load with the flyers themselves being approximately three tsons. Photo shows the T+2 leaving the field. 5/2/23
PHOTO OF- AUSTRALIAN INVENTOR HERE WITH PLANE WHICH RISES VERTICALLY INTO AIR.

NEWS ITEM—William J. Beach, an Australian inventor, is shown here with his model of an aeroplane which risks vertically into the air, sustaining itself by rapidly revolving horizontal propellers. Mr. Beach believes that his machine, when built in normal proportions, stands a good chance of winning the $100,000 prize offered by the Agro Club of France for the first machines which proves itself capable of rising vertically into air.

COLLANDER OF LOST PLANS FOR WHICH PACIFIC IS SCOURED.

S/120Al00 --Commander John Rodgers, leader of the Pacific expedition which not with disaster this week. On Monday, August 31st, two giant naval planes the P.N.9 No.1 and the P.N.9 No.3 hopped off from San Transisco in an attempt to make a new non-stop flying record by sailing to Hawaii, a distance of 2100 nautical miles. The route had been carefully mapped out by the Navy Department, and warships stationed all the way to Hawaii at 200 miles intervals. During the first few hundred miles, the two pioneer planes flew steadily eastward, with every prospect for a new record. But on the afternoon of Tuesday, the second day out, Commander Wilbur R. Van Auken of the U.S.S. Aroostook, reported that he had lost touch with Commander Rodgers plane, while the second plane, P.N.9 No.3 had been forced down for lack of fuel. Since Tuesday no word has been received as to the whereabouts of Rogers and his 4 co-aviators, despite the thorough search being carried on by both naval and private boats, airships, etc. In spite of the continued failure to locate the missing plane, the Navy Department reiterates its hope of rescuing him, and has sent telegrams of encouragement to relatives of the lost aviators. It is believed that if the plane was forced to descend to the water, and in the descent was not capsized, it should still be afloat.
shows Commander Rodgers photographed in his plane, the now missing P.N.9 No.1, shortly before setting out on the Hawaiian cruise.

59665 EXPERIMENT WHEREIN TWO AIRPLANES
FLY IN VERY CLOSE PROXIMITY

Lawrence B. Sperry, President of the Lawrence Sperry Aircraft Corp. has demonstrated that it is possible for two airplanes to fly, "one above the other at precisely the same speed, so that, relative to each other, they are motionless. The experiments which Mr. Sperry has been carrying on are of great commercial importance in the aeronautic world as it will facilitate the transference of cargoes from long trip planes to smaller planes of local lines. Photo shows: Mr. Sperry who piloted the "Little Messenger" and Capt. Clyde Finter, pilot of the DeHaviland used in the experiment. 3/8/23
